title: The Work of Staying
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 32 of 40
content:
The application had been sitting under the car wash receipts for two days.

Greg wasn't snooping. He was looking for the electricity bill, which was somehow more embarrassing. He lifted the envelope, saw my name, and put it back on the table without opening it.

"That looks important," he said.

"It is."

"Want to tell me?"

I looked at the plastic chair across from him. I wanted to say it wasn't decided, which was true, and leave the rest until I knew what I wanted. But he would notice me being careful with every word.

"I got offered a job," I said. "Not here."

He smiled immediately. "That's fantastic."

"It's across the water. I'd have to spend longer stretches away from Beach City."

"Still fantastic."

The fluorescent light buzzed above us. I watched him straighten a stack of receipts that didn't need straightening.

"Greg."

"What?"

"You can be happy for me and still have feelings about the distance."

He stopped moving. "I know."

"Then why are you pretending this is as easy as finding a new parking spot?"

He looked down. "Because I was afraid if I said I'd miss you, it'd sound like I was asking you to give it up."

There it was. The thing beneath the joke. I pulled out the other chair.

"Sit?"

He sat. The electricity bill fell from his hand and landed upside down between us.

"I'm not asking permission," I said. "I am asking whether you want to talk about what this would mean for us."

"Yeah. I do."

We started with the stupidly practical parts because they were the parts we could actually do something about. The job paid enough to cover travel if I didn't spend it all getting back and forth for one-night visits. Greg had bookings on certain weekends, including a school fundraiser he'd already promised to play. I had other partners and commitments beyond Beach City; none of those disappeared because a job offer existed.

"I know you've been clear about being ethically non-monogamous," he said. "And that you prefer polyamory. I guess I keep thinking a schedule's gonna make me sound like I'm booking a slot in your life."

"You are in my life. A schedule just means I don't promise to be in two places on the same Thursday."

He laughed softly. "That'd make a good song."

"Only if you leave the receipts out of it."

We wrote down what we could promise. We would tell each other about changes early enough to matter. Neither of us would treat silence as a punishment. We could say we wanted more time without using guilt to get it. Visits would be invitations, not surprise tests. If either of us couldn't make something work, we would talk about it instead of announcing a failure.

Greg pointed at the page. "This feels very grown-up."

"Terrifying, isn't it?"

"I was hoping love came with fewer columns."

I nudged his knee with mine. "You have a business. You know columns."

"That's different. The columns at the car wash don't have feelings."

"Your accounts would suggest otherwise."

He laughed, then went quiet.

"I do want you to stay," he said. "I know I don't get to decide for you. But I want you to know that."

The admission made my throat tighten. There was something braver about hearing his preference without having to fight for my freedom first.

"Thank you," I said. "I haven't decided."

"Okay."

"And if I take the job, I still want to come home here sometimes. Not because I owe you proof. Because I like this stupid office and your terrible coffee."

"Hey. The coffee is improving."

"It's learning to apologize."

He reached across the table. "Can I hold your hand?"

"Yes."

We sat with our fingers tangled between the bill and the job application. He didn't ask to see the letter. I didn't hand it over to prove I trusted him.

After closing, we walked to the van. The air had turned cool. A light flickered in the car wash sign, and he made a note to call someone about it before the next wet morning.

Inside the van, he put on a quiet recording—not one of the old songs that felt too loaded, but a rough instrumental he'd made the previous week. I leaned against his shoulder.

"Stay for dinner?" he asked.

"Yes. Tonight."

"Tonight's pretty good."

He kissed me when I turned toward him. We had all the time we wanted for that moment, and no right to assume anything about the next one. Later, we went inside and let the night become ours.

In the morning, the application was still unanswered. I put it in the drawer beside my toothbrush. We would talk again when I knew more, not pretend a single night could settle a whole future.
